[[File:Getty USGS.jpg|upright|thumb|[[United States Geological Survey|USGS]] satellite image of the Getty Center. The circular building to the left is the Getty Research Institute. The two buildings at the top are the Getty Trust administrative offices and the rest is the Museum.]]
The '''Getty Research Institute''' ('''GRI'''), located at the [[Getty Center]] in [[Los Angeles]], California, is "dedicated to furthering knowledge and advancing understanding of the visual arts".<ref name=GRI>[http://www.getty.edu/research/institute/ About the Research Institute (Research at the Getty)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607104131/http://www.getty.edu/research/institute/ |date=2011-06-07 }} Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref> 

A program of the [[J. Paul Getty Trust]], GRI maintains a research library, organizes exhibitions and other events, sponsors a residential scholars program, publishes books, and produces electronic databases (Getty Publications).<ref name=GRI/>

==History==

The GRI was originally called the "'''Getty Center for the History of Art and the Humanities'''", and was first discussed in 1983.<ref>Isenberg, Barbara. Manuscripts rated top Getty acquisition. ''Los Angeles Times'',  p. H1, March 10, 1983.</ref> It was located in [[Santa Monica, California|Santa Monica]]<ref>[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9807E0DA1E38F930A15757C0A963948260 Getty Center acquires sculptor's archive.] ''New York Times'', April 23, 1985. Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref> and its first director (beginning in 1985) was [[Kurt W. Forster]].<ref name=Muchnic92>Muchnic, Suzanne. Getty Center's Kurt Forster resigns post. ''Los Angeles Times'', p. 6, March 20, 1992.</ref>  GRI's library had 30,000 volumes in 1983, but grew to 450,000 volumes by 1986.<ref name=Muchnic86/>

In a statement upon his departure in 1992, Forster summarized his tenure as "Beginning with the rudiments of a small museum library... the center grew... to become one of the nation's preeminent research centers for arts and culture...".<ref name=Muchnic92/> In 1994, [[Salvatore Settis]], a professor of the history of classical art and archeology in Italy, became the director of the Center.<ref>Briefing - Italian professor to join Getty. ''Daily News of Los Angeles'', March 9, 1993.</ref>  By 1996, the Center's name had been changed to "Getty Research Institute for the History of Art and the Humanities",<ref name=Scholars96>[http://www.getty.edu/news/press/scholar/laschol.html Getty Research Institute for the History of Art and the Humanities Announces 1996-97 Getty Scholars.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607104157/http://www.getty.edu/news/press/scholar/laschol.html |date=2011-06-07 }} Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref> and by 1999 it was known simply as "Getty Research Institute".<ref>[http://www.getty.edu/news/press/scholar/grischo99.html The Getty Research Institute Announces 1999-2000 Getty Scholars.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607104201/http://www.getty.edu/news/press/scholar/grischo99.html |date=2011-06-07 }} September 7, 1999. Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref>

When the Getty Information Institute (formerly the Art History Information Program, established in 1983) was dissolved in 1999 as a "result of a change of leadership at the Getty Trust",<ref>Fink, Eleanor E.  [http://www.dlib.org/dlib/march99/fink/03fink.html  The Getty Information Institute. A retrospective.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220202102402/http://dlib.org/dlib/march99/fink/03fink.html |date=2022-02-02 }} ''[[D-Lib Magazine]]'', March 1999, Volume 5, Issue 3. Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref> GRI absorbed "many of its functions".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://library.getty.edu/cgi-bin/Pwebrecon.cgi?v1=10&ti=1,10&SL=B&DATE=&DTBL=E&DATE2=&LANG=ENG%7C0&PID=gzFY_fZ6HeqAI5t2nuU5SwpiUJJcB&SEQ=20110618025451&SID=1 |title=Getty Research Institute. Records, 1991-1999 |access-date=June 18, 2011 |work=Library Catalog Entry |publisher=Getty Trust }}{{dead link|date=January 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-83841990.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121106052921/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-83841990.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=November 6, 2012|title=Getty Trust Plans Moves to Cut Costs, Raise Funds|date=October 6, 1998|work=Los Angeles Daily News|first=Reed |last=Johnson|via=[[HighBeam Research]]|url-access=subscription|location=Los Angeles, CA|access-date=June 18, 2011}}</ref>

In 2000, [[Thomas E. Crow]] was selected as GRI director to replace Settis who had resigned in 1999.<ref>Encore - short subjects. Getty's choice. ''Orange County Register'', February 20, 2000.</ref> Crow announced in October 2006 that he would be leaving for [[New York University]].<ref name=NewDirGaehtgens>[http://www.getty.edu/news/press/center/gaehtgens_release_081407.html Thomas W. Gaehtgens named director of the Getty Research Institute.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110625042449/http://www.getty.edu/news/press/center/gaehtgens_release_081407.html |date=2011-06-25 }} August 14, 2007. Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref>  In November 2007 [[Thomas W. Gaehtgens]] became GRI's director;<ref>Associated Press.  "German art historian to head Getty's research institute in LA." ''International Herald Tribune'', August 14, 2007.</ref> he was previously (1985–86) a visiting scholar with the Getty Center for the History of Art and the Humanities.<ref name=Muchnic86/><ref name=NewDirGaehtgens/> He served in the position until 2019 when [[Mary Miller (art historian)|Mary Miller]] was appointed as the new GRI director.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_18.pdf|title=J. Paul Getty Trust Report 2018|access-date=November 9, 2020|page=5|archive-date=April 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416200511/http://www.getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_18.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Programs==

===Library===
[[File:Inside the Getty Research Institute.jpg|thumb|300px|Inside the Getty Research Institute Library]]
Among other holdings, GRI's research library contains over 1 million volumes of books, periodicals, and auction catalogs; special collections; and two million photographs of art and architecture.<ref>[http://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/library/index.html Research Library Overview (Research at the Getty).] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060107174910/http://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/library/index.html |date=2006-01-07 }} Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref>

The library is located at the [[Getty Center]], and does not circulate its collections, but does extend library privileges to any visitor.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.getty.edu/research/library/using/access/index.html|title=Library Access and Reader Privileges|publisher=Getty Trust|access-date=May 25, 2011|archive-date=June 7, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607190006/http://www.getty.edu/research/library/using/access/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Exhibitions and other events===
GRI holds two public exhibitions per year in its two galleries which "focus primarily on the special collections of the Research Library or on work produced by artists in residence".<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Getty Research Institute|url=http://getty.edu/research/exhibitions/|title=Exhibitions|access-date=September 2, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081006065325/http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions/|archive-date=October 6, 2008}}</ref>  For example, in 2005–2006 GRI held an exhibition entitled "[[Julius Shulman]], Modernity and the Metropolis".<ref name=Shulman>Getty Research Institute. [http://www.getty.edu/art/exhibitions/shulman/  Julius Shulman, modernity and the metropolis. October 11, 2005 - January 22, 2006.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081006063742/http://www.getty.edu/art/exhibitions/shulman/ |date=October 6, 2008 }} Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref> The exhibition traveled to the [[National Building Museum]]<ref>National Building Museum. [https://web.archive.org/web/20080907063644/http://www.nbm.org/exhibitions-collections/exhibitions/julius-shulman.html Julius Shulman: modernity and the metropolis.] April 1, 2006 - July 30, 2006. Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref> and to the [[Art Institute of Chicago]].<ref>Art Institute of Chicago. [http://www.artic.edu/aic/exhibitions/exhibition/shulman Julius Shulman: modernity and the metropolis.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061201093310/http://www.artic.edu/aic/exhibitions/exhibition/shulman |date=2006-12-01 }} September 2, 2006 - December 3, 2006. Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref> Other GRI exhibitions have included "Overdrive: L.A. Constructs the Future, 1940-1990", co-organized with the museum in 2013,<ref>{{cite web |title=Overdrive: L.A. Constructs the Future, 1940-1990 |url=https://www.getty.edu/art/exhibitions/overdrive/ |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=20 January 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209172640/http://www.getty.edu/art/exhibitions/overdrive/ |url-status=live }}</ref> "World War I: War of Images, Images of War" in 2015,<ref>{{cite web |title=World War I: War of Images, Images of War |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/exhibitions/ww1/ |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=20 January 2021 |archive-date=11 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210211012321/https://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/exhibitions/ww1/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and "Cave Temples of Dunhuang: Buddhist Art on China's Silk Road", co-organized with Getty Conservation Institute in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cave Temples of Dunhuang |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/exhibitions/cave_temples_dunhuang/index.html |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=20 January 2021 |archive-date=25 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125142808/http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/exhibitions/cave_temples_dunhuang/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In addition to exhibitions, GRI organizes lectures (open to the public), colloquia (most open to the public), workshops (by invitation only), and screenings of films and videos (open to the public).<ref>Getty Research Institute. [http://getty.edu/research/scholarly_activities/events/colloquia.html Colloquia, lectures, and workshops.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081014072937/http://getty.edu/research/scholarly_activities/events/colloquia.html |date=2008-10-14 }} Retrieved September 2, 2008.</ref>

GRI also holds online exhibitions. In 2017 it launched its first online-only exhibition, "The Legacy of Ancient Palmyra".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Farago |first1=Jason |title=The Ancient Syrian City ISIS is Destroying, Preserved Online |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/15/arts/design/palmyra-syria-isis.html |access-date=15 December 2020 |work=New York Times |date=17 February 2017 |archive-date=2 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202042058/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/15/arts/design/palmyra-syria-isis.html |url-status=live }}</ref> This exhibition was relaunched in 2021 as "Return to Palmyra" with new content and Arabic translations.<ref>{{cite news |title=Return to Palmyra |url=https://www.apollo-magazine.com/return-to-palmyra/ |access-date=18 February 2021 |publisher=Apollo The International Art Magazine |date=February 5, 2021 |archive-date=14 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214144217/https://www.apollo-magazine.com/return-to-palmyra/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Its next online exhibition was "Bauhaus: Building the New Artist", which was launched in 2019 in tandem with its gallery exhibition "Bauhaus Beginnings".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gelt |first1=Jessica |title=Get your Bauhaus on with interactive art in the Getty's new online exhibition |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/arts/la-et-cm-bauhaus-online-exhibition-getty-20190702-story.html |access-date=15 December 2020 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=2 July 2019 |archive-date=7 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107231400/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/arts/la-et-cm-bauhaus-online-exhibition-getty-20190702-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2013 the GRI gallery underwent a renovation that added an additional 2,000 square feet to its existing 800 square feet of space.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stephan |first1=Annelisa |title=Gallery at the Getty Research Institute Undergoing Dramatic Expansion |url=https://blogs.getty.edu/iris/gallery-at-the-getty-research-institute-undergoing-dramatic-expansion/ |website=Getty Iris |access-date=15 December 2020 |archive-date=1 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201061937/http://blogs.getty.edu/iris/gallery-at-the-getty-research-institute-undergoing-dramatic-expansion/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Residential scholars program===
The residential scholars program seeks to "integrate the often isolated territory of art history into the wider sphere of the humanities".<ref name=Muchnic86>Muchnic, Suzanne. Getty's visiting guinea pig scholars. ''Los Angeles Times'', p. 98, August 10, 1986.</ref>  The first class of scholars arrived in 1985–1986; they had their salaries paid for and their housing provided but were under "absolutely no obligation to produce," a policy that continues to this day.<ref name=Muchnic86/> Among the notable scholars was German writer [[Christa Wolf]] in 1992–1993, who wrote the novel ''Medea: a modern retelling'' during her year at GRI.<ref>Gitlin, Todd. [https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F0CE2DF1330F937A35757C0A965958260 "I did not imagine that I lived in truth".] ''New York Times'', April 4, 1993. Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref><ref>Wolf, Christa. ''Medea: a modern retelling''. New York: Nan A. Talese, 1998. {{ISBN|0-385-49060-7}}</ref><ref>Slavitt, David R.  [https://www.nytimes.com/books/98/06/14/reviews/980614.14slavitt.html Revenge fantasy. Christa Wolf puts a late-20th-century spin on the story of Jason and Medea.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170316181553/http://www.nytimes.com/books/98/06/14/reviews/980614.14slavitt.html |date=2017-03-16 }} ''New York Times'', June 14, 1998. Retrieved September 2, 2008. (paid site)</ref>

Each year the scholars are invited to work on projects related to an annual theme.<ref name=GRITheme>Getty Research Institute. [http://getty.edu/research/scholars/years/index.html Past Themes & Scholars.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607153058/http://www.getty.edu/research/scholars/years/index.html |date=2011-06-07 }} Retrieved May 25, 2011.</ref> The lengths of stay vary: Getty scholars are in residence for three, six or nine months,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/getty_scholars.html|title=Getty Scholar Grants|publisher=Getty Trust|access-date=May 26, 2011|archive-date=June 7, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607211554/http://www.getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/getty_scholars.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> visiting scholars for one to three months,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/library_research_grants.html|title=Library Research Grants|publisher=Getty Trust|access-date=May 26, 2011|archive-date=June 7, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607211759/http://www.getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/library_research_grants.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> and predoctoral and postdoctoral fellows for a nine-month academic year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/getty_pre_postdoctoral_fellowships.html|title=Pre- and Postdoctoral Fellowships|publisher=Getty Trust|access-date=May 26, 2011|archive-date=June 7, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607212213/http://www.getty.edu/foundation/funding/residential/getty_pre_postdoctoral_fellowships.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Publications===
GRI publishes "Series Imprints" books in the categories of "Issues and Debates", "Texts & Documents", "Introduction To" (on "cultural heritage information in electronic form"), and "ReSources" (on the library's special collections).<ref name=Publications>Getty Research Institute. [http://www.getty.edu/research/institute/publications.html Publications Overview.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080514130427/http://www.getty.edu/research/institute/publications.html |date=2008-05-14 }} Retrieved September 2, 2008.</ref>  In addition, GRI publishes exhibition catalogs and other materials in hardcopy form.<ref name=Publications/>

In 2021, ''[[Käthe Kollwitz]]: Prints, Process, Politics'' (edited by Louis Marchesano, {{ISBN|978-1-60606-615-7}}), which accompanied an exhibition of the same name that ran at GRI and the Art Institute of Chicago between 2019 and 2020, won the College Art Association's Alfred H. Barr Jr. Award for distinguished catalogues in the history of art.<ref>{{cite web |title=Awards for Distinction |url=https://www.collegeart.org/programs/awards/barr |website=CAA |access-date=1 March 2021 |archive-date=28 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928115754/https://www.collegeart.org/programs/awards/barr |url-status=live }}</ref> 

GRI publishes a peer-reviewed academic journal, the ''Getty Research Journal'', that presents work "related to the Getty's collections, initiatives, and research".<ref>{{cite web |title=Getty Research Journal |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/publications/grj/ |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=15 December 2020 |archive-date=19 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201219184807/https://www.getty.edu/research/publications/grj/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Started in 2009, the journal publishes one annual issue and is slated to begin biannual publication in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Getty Research Journal |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/publications/grj/ |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=15 December 2020 |archive-date=19 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201219184807/https://www.getty.edu/research/publications/grj/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Electronic databases===
Among the electronic databases from the former Getty Information Institute that GRI continues to produce are:
* [[Getty Vocabulary Program]] databases ([[Art & Architecture Thesaurus]] (AAT), [[Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names]] (TGN), and [[Union List of Artist Names]] (ULAN))<ref>Getty Research Institute. [http://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/vocabularies/ Learn about the Getty Vocabularies.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100720221843/https://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/vocabularies/training.html |date=2010-07-20 }} Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref>
* Bibliography of the History of Art (BHA)<ref>Getty Research Institute. [http://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/bha/ Bibliography of the History of Art.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609040427/http://www.getty.edu/research/conducting_research/bha/ |date=2008-06-09 }} Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref>
* '''Getty Provenance Index''' which holds records of collections, auction sales and other information for researching the art market and the [[provenance]] of works.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.getty.edu/research/tools/provenance/ |title=Collecting and Provenance Research, Retrieved August 26, 2011. |access-date=August 24, 2011 |archive-date=August 6, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110806062230/http://www.getty.edu/research/tools/provenance/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
*The '''Getty Research Portal''' provides free access to fully digitized art history texts in the public domain. The database launched in 2012 and is a collaboration with libraries that are digitizing art history books. Initial contributors include the Avery Architectural & Fine Arts Library at Columbia University, the Biblioteca de la Universidad de Málaga, the Frick Art Reference Library, the Getty Research Institute, the Heidelberg University Library, the Institut national d'histoire de l'art, members of the New York Art Resources Consortium, and the Thomas J. Watson Library at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.<ref>{{cite web|title=Getty Research Portal|url=http://www.getty.edu/research/tools/portal/index.html|publisher=Getty Research Institute|access-date=18 February 2014|archive-date=26 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140326194239/http://www.getty.edu/research/tools/portal/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref> 
In 2006, GRI and the OCLC [[Online Computer Library Center]] announced that the Getty Vocabularies ([[Art & Architecture Thesaurus]], [[Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names]], and [[Union List of Artist Names]]) will be available as a Web service.<ref>OCLC Online Computer Library Center, Inc. [http://www.oclc.org/news/releases/200642.htm Getty Vocabularies added to OCLC Terminologies Service.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081026055623/http://www.oclc.org/news/releases/200642.htm |date=2008-10-26 }} November 9, 2006. Retrieved May 26, 2011.</ref>

Until July 1, 2009, the Getty Information Institute and later GRI co-produced the Avery Index to Architectural Periodicals with the [[Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library]]. On that date, GRI transferred the database back to [[Columbia University]], which continues to maintain it.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://library.columbia.edu/news/libraries/2009/20090701_averyindex.html|title=Avery Index Returns to Columbia University|publisher=Columbia University|date=July 1, 2009|access-date=May 26, 2011|archive-date=July 27, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727135721/http://library.columbia.edu/news/libraries/2009/20090701_averyindex.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The Getty Research Institute also participates in the [[German/American Provenance Research Exchange Program]] (PREP), which trains researchers specializing in Holocaust-era provenance projects.<ref>{{cite web|title=German/American Provenance Research Exchange Program (PREP) for Museum Professionals, 2017-2019|url=http://www.lootedart.com/S4ILLS305441|website=lootedart.com|access-date=25 August 2017|archive-date=25 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825103034/http://www.lootedart.com/S4ILLS305441|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Special collections==
GRI holds many important archives related to artists, architects, and art collectors. It also houses the institutional archives of past and current programs of Getty Trust.<ref>{{cite web |title=Institutional Archives |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/institutional_archives/index.html |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=25 January 2021 |archive-date=12 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412193346/https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/institutional_archives/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Already by 1985, the Getty had acquired the complete archive of the American sculptor [[Malvina Hoffman]]. In 2011, it acquired [[Harald Szeemann]]’s substantial archive, consisting of more than 1,000 boxes of correspondence, research files, drawings, and ephemera, as well as some 28,000 books and 36,000 photographs.<ref>Kate Taylor (June 7, 2011), [http://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/06/07/getty-acquires-vast-archive-of-post-war-art-documents/ Getty Acquires Vast Archive of Post-War Art Documents] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130405145904/http://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/06/07/getty-acquires-vast-archive-of-post-war-art-documents/ |date=2013-04-05 }} ''[[New York Times]]''.</ref> It also owns several art dealers' archives, including records for the [[Goupil & Cie]] and [[Boussod Valadon]] galleries, Knoedler Gallery, and the [[Duveen Brothers]].<ref>Carol Vogel (October 18, 2012), [https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/19/arts/design/getty-institute-buys-knoedler-gallery-archive.html Getty Institute Buys Knoedler Gallery Archive] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170314160540/http://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/19/arts/design/getty-institute-buys-knoedler-gallery-archive.html |date=2017-03-14 }} ''[[New York Times]]''.</ref> It also owns the papers of gallery owner Clara Diament Sujo and the records of Stendhal Art Galleries.<ref>{{cite web |title=Latin American Dealer Archives |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/notable/LAD.html |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=25 January 2021 |archive-date=10 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210073438/https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/notable/LAD.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The GRI’s Special Collections includes archives of major modern and contemporary artists and movements. In 2019 it acquired the complete archives of sculptor [[Claes Oldenburg]] and his wife [[Coosje van Bruggen]].<ref>{{cite news|last=The Associated Press|first1=|date=April 9, 2019|title=Getty Research Institute acquires Claes Oldenburg archives|work=|publisher=Seattle Times|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/entertainment/getty-research-institute-acquires-claes-oldenburg-archives/|access-date=25 January 2021|archive-date=17 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917102147/https://www.seattletimes.com/entertainment/getty-research-institute-acquires-claes-oldenburg-archives/|url-status=live}}</ref> It has collecting strengths in early twentieth-century European modern art movements including [[Dada]] and [[Surrealism]], Italian [[Futurism]], Russian [[Modernism]], and [[Bauhaus]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Major Collecting Areas |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/highlights/index.html |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=25 January 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209171632/https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/highlights/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Additionally, the GRI's holdings in the field of experimental art includes archives related to many important mid-century 20th-century movements and groups, including the Japanese avant-garde, [[Fluxus]], [[Experiments in Art and Technology]] (E.A.T.), and the [[Situationist International]]. It also holds papers relating to music, dance, and film media, including the papers of composer [[David Tudor]], the archives of dancers [[Simone Forti]] and [[Yvonne Rainer]], the Long Beach Museum of Art video archive, and the recordings of the New York performance space [[The Kitchen (art institution)|The Kitchen]].

GRI has significant archives in feminist art, including the papers of the activist group [[Guerrilla Girls]] and feminist conceptual artist [[Mary Kelly (artist)|Mary Kelly]]. It also owns the video archives of the [[Woman's Building (Los Angeles)|Woman's Building]], a Los Angeles-based arts and education center. In 2018 GRI received a grant through the Save America's Treasures program to process and digitize 11 archives related to the Woman's Building, including the records of Feminist Art Workers, Sisters for Survival, Mother Art, [[The Waitresses (artists)|the Waitresses]], [[Barbara T. Smith]], [[Faith Wilding]], and [[Nancy Buchanan]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Getty Research Institute Awarded a "Save America's Treasures" Grant to Process and Digitize Archives of the Woman's Building |url=http://news.getty.edu/content/1208/files/Woman%27s%20Building%20IMLS%20FINAL%20(002).pdf |website=News from the Getty |access-date=25 January 2021 |archive-date=2 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202121130/http://news.getty.edu/content/1208/files/Woman%27s%20Building%20IMLS%20FINAL%20%28002%29.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the field of performance art, the GRI collections include the papers of [[Allan Kaprow]] and [[Rachel Rosenthal]], as well as [[Robert R. McElroy]], who photographically documented many early [[Happening|“Happenings”]]. It also has the records of High Performance magazine and the [[Los Angeles Contemporary Exhibitions]] (LACE) space.

GRI houses archives of several major mid-century, California-based architects, including [[Frank Gehry]], [[Paul R. Williams]], [[John Lautner]], [[Ray Kappe]], and [[William Krisel]]. In addition, it has the papers of architectural photographers [[Lucien Hervé]] and [[Julius Shulman]]. It also has the collections of architectural critic [[Ada Louise Huxtable]] and architectural historian [[Thomas Hines (architectural historian)|Thomas S. Hines]].

GRI’s photography collections include the work of French darkroom pioneer [[Louis Rousselet]] and the 19th-century travel photographs of [[Honoré Théodoric d'Albert de Luynes|Honoré d’Albert, VIII Duc de Luynes]]. It owns collections of the work of German and Hungarian collaborators [[Shunk-Kender]], German-Argentine photographer [[Grete Stern]], and Venezuelan art critic and photographer [[Alfredo Boulton]]. Additionally, it also has archives of American photographers [[Robert Mapplethorpe]] and [[Allan Sekula]], as well as those of magazine editor [[Alexander Liberman]].  

GRI owns over 27,000 prints from as early as the 16th century.<ref>{{cite web |title=Prints--Special Collections |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/highlights/prints/index.html |website=Getty Research Institute |access-date=25 January 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209190327/https://www.getty.edu/research/special_collections/highlights/prints/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> These include a complete set of the oeuvre of [[Giovanni Battista Piranesi]] and the ''Speculum romanae magnificentiae'' of [[Antonio Lafreri]]. It also has significant prints from China during the Qing dynasty, including ''Complete Map of the World'' by [[Ferdinand Verbiest]], ''Battles of the Emperor of China'', and ''Garden of Perfect Clarity''. It also has a collection of rare botanical books and woodblocks from the 16th through 19th centuries belonging to Tania Norris.

The GRI collections also possess sketchbooks of many important artists, including [[Francesco di Giorgio Martini]], [[Jacques-Louis David]], [[Charles Percier]], [[Adolph Menzel]], [[Félix Bracquemond]], [[Edmond Aman-Jean]], [[Ernst Ludwig Kirchner]], [[Malvina Hoffman]], [[Diego Rivera]], and [[Mark Rothko]].

==Research projects and initiatives==
Among GRI's special projects was "L.A. as Subject: The Transformative Culture of Los Angeles Communities" conducted between 1995 and 1999, whose purposes included "enhanc[ing] existing resources and develop new resources that support new research scholarship on LA and also encourag[ing] the preservation, conservation, and display of local material culture".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/events/lasubject/overview.html|publisher=Getty Research Institute|title=L.A. as Subject. Overview.|year=1999|access-date=May 25, 2011|archive-date=October 9, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121009203325/http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/events/lasubject/overview.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>  

In collaboration with local organizations, GRI published ''Cultural Inheritance/L.A.: A Resource Directory of Less Visible Archives and Collections in the Los Angeles Region'' in 1999.<ref>Johnson, Reed. Getty helping bring L.A. history together. ''Daily News of Los Angeles'', June 8, 1999.</ref> In 2000, the L.A. as Subject project was transferred to the [[University of Southern California]], which continues to update and expand an online version of the resource directory.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/events/lasubject/index.html|publisher=Getty Research Institute|title=L.A. as Subject. Home.|access-date=May 25, 2011|archive-date=December 16, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101216162606/http://www.getty.edu/research/exhibitions_events/events/lasubject/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Pacific Standard Time, one of Getty's most ambitious and important ongoing projects, began as a 2002 initiative between GRI and Getty Foundation meant to preserve postwar Los Angeles art history that risked being lost or inaccessible. It grew out of an oral history project at GRI and was initially called "On the Record."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Finkel |first1=Jori |title=Galleries join 'Pacific Standard Time'; The fall's big study of regional art history expands to include a mosaic of gallery contributions |work=Los Angeles Times |date=January 20, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Muchnic |first1=Suzanne |title=Getty grants unite SoCal arts; Organizations working on a regionwide historical project will share $3.1 million |work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref> At first the initiative consisted of grants to local museums and libraries as well as GRI acquiring "papers, videos, photographs, and other records from the period."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dobrzynski |first1=Judith H. |title=A Cultural Conversation With James N. Wood: Easing The Getty Into Young Adulthood |publisher=Wall Street Journal |date=January 20, 2009}}</ref>

The first set of Pacific Standard Time exhibitions, called "[[Pacific Standard Time: Art in L.A., 1945-1980]]," was coordinated between Getty and other Los Angeles museums between 2011 and 2012. Over 60 institutions who were awarded grants totaling about $10 million participated by presenting exhibitions and programs on California art history.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Roberta |title=A New Pin On the Art Map |issue=Late Edition (East Coast) |work=New York Times |date=November 13, 2011}}</ref> The second iteration of Pacific Standard Time was "Modern Architecture in L.A." in 2013. The third set of exhibitions was "[[Pacific Standard Time: LA/LA]]" in 2017-2018, which sought to place Los Angeles and Latin American art in dialogue. This iteration extended beyond modern and contemporary art to include exhibitions on the ancient and pre-modern eras.<ref>{{cite web |title=About PST: LA/LA |url=http://www.pacificstandardtime.org/lala/en/about/index.html |website=Pacific Standard Time: LA/LA |access-date=21 January 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426135848/http://www.pacificstandardtime.org/lala/en/about/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation's Institute for Applied Economics found that LA/LA "created over 4,000 jobs, added $430 million in economic output [to] the regional economy, and supported labor income (wages) of nearly $188 million."<ref>{{cite web |title=Getty-led Pacific Standard Time: LA/LA Created Over 4,000 Jobs and Celebrated Latin American and Latino Art |url=https://laedc.org/2018/05/01/getty-pacific-standard-time-economic-impact/#:~:text=LAEDC's%20Institute%20for%20Applied%20Economics,million%20in%20economic%20output%20the |website=Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation |access-date=21 January 2021 |archive-date=28 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210128140253/https://laedc.org/2018/05/01/getty-pacific-standard-time-economic-impact/#:~:text=LAEDC's%20Institute%20for%20Applied%20Economics,million%20in%20economic%20output%20the |url-status=live }}</ref>

One of the major impacts of Pacific Standard Time was that it established Los Angeles and the west coast, not just New York City, as a major center of art production in the postwar United States.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Roberta |title=A New Pin On the Art Map |issue=Late Edition (East Coast) |work=New York Times |date=November 13, 2011}}</ref> ''ARTnews'' named Pacific Standard Time as the most important art exhibition of the 2010s.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Durón |first1=Maximilíano |last2=Greenberger |first2=Alex |title=The Most Important Art Exhibitions of the 2010s |url=https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/most-important-exhibitions-2010s-1202672433/2/ |access-date=21 January 2021 |publisher=ARTnews |date=December 17, 2019 |archive-date=19 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211219075223/https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/most-important-exhibitions-2010s-1202672433/2/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2011 GRI acquired [[Edward Ruscha|Ed Ruscha's]] Streets of Los Angeles archive, which includes "thousands of negatives, hundreds of photographic contact sheets, and related documents and ephemera."<ref>{{cite web |title=The Getty Acquires Ed Ruscha Photographs and Archives |url=http://news.getty.edu/the-getty-acquires-ed-ruscha-photographs-and-archive.htm |website=Getty |access-date=21 January 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209171916/http://news.getty.edu/the-getty-acquires-ed-ruscha-photographs-and-archive.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2020 GRI launched the website "12 Sunsets: Exploring Ed Ruscha's Archive," which compiles over 65,000 photographs that Ruscha took of buildings along [[Sunset Boulevard]] between 1965 and 2007.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vankin |first1=Deborah |title=65,000 photos of Sunset Boulevard: Take the ultimate road trip with Ed Ruscha |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-10-07/ed-ruscha-sunset-boulevard-getty-database |access-date=21 January 2021 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=October 7, 2020 |archive-date=2021-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217070943/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-10-07/ed-ruscha-sunset-boulevard-getty-database |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2018 GRI announced the African American Art History Initiative, which seeks to "strengthen its African-American holdings through key archival acquisitions,"<ref>{{cite news |last1=Finkel |first1=Jori |title=African-American Art Is Focus of Getty Project |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/25/arts/design/getty-african-american-art-history-initiative.html |access-date=21 January 2021 |work=New York Times |date=September 27, 2018 |archive-date=9 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201109025039/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/25/arts/design/getty-african-american-art-history-initiative.html |url-status=live }}</ref> beginning with the acquisition of the archive of assemblage artist [[Betye Saar]].

GRI is funding a digitization of "The General History of the Things of New Spain", also known as the [[Florentine Codex]], a 16th-century illuminated manuscript written in Nahuatl and Spanish describing Aztec life in what is now Mexico City at the time of the Spanish conquest.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Miranda |first1=Carolina A. |title=How a vital record of Mexican indigenous life was created under quarantine |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-03-26/coronavirus-florentine-codex-mexican-indigenous-life-smallpox-quarantine |access-date=21 January 2021 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 26, 2020 |archive-date=2021-01-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121125806/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-03-26/coronavirus-florentine-codex-mexican-indigenous-life-smallpox-quarantine |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Employees and budget==
During the period July 2006 – June 2007, GRI had approximately 200 full-time and part-time employees, and a budget of $63.7 million.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_07.pdf|title=The J. Paul Getty Trust 2007 report|access-date=June 17, 2011|page=76|archive-date=July 16, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716140615/http://getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_07.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Between July 2017 – June 2018, its budget was $68.6 million.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_18.pdf|title=J. Paul Getty Trust Report 2018|access-date=December 15, 2020|page=144|archive-date=April 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416200511/http://www.getty.edu/about/governance/trustreport/trust_report_18.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>
